title: Project 1: command-line calculator
learningObjectives: Explain the topic and its C rules.

understand.concept: A command-line calculator combines input parsing, arithmetic operations, validation and formatted output. It should reject malformed expressions and handle division by zero before performing the operation.
understand.whyItMatters: A small project tests whether the learner can combine functions, types, control flow and input validation into one coherent program.
understand.analogy: Treat the project or language feature as a set of components with explicit interfaces and responsibilities.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal language, library and resource-management rules.

explain.narrative:
A command-line calculator combines input parsing, arithmetic operations, validation and formatted output. It should reject malformed expressions and handle division by zero before performing the operation.

For a complete implementation, define input constraints, ownership, error handling and test cases before coding. Compile with warnings and verify normal, boundary and failure behaviour.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The program checks that three input fields were converted, rejects a zero divisor and dispatches on the operator. A production calculator should also define numeric range, trailing input and floating-point error policies.

practise.independentTask: Extend the calculator with a loop, a quit command and tests for invalid operators and malformed input.
hints: Check scanf's assignment count before using the variables.
Floating-point division by zero and integer division by zero have different language and environment considerations; define a deliberate policy.
Separate parsing, calculation and display into functions.
